researchPapers.title: Bull Shark (Carcharhinus leucas) Occurrence along Beaches of South-Eastern Australia: Understanding Where, When, and Why
keyFindings: Bull Sharks are the primary species responsible for most shark incidents in Sydney region
Rainfall events are a critical driver - Bull Sharks actively move into estuarine and coastal areas after significant rainfall (>30-40mm)
Water temperature above 18-20°C correlates with increased Bull Shark presence in nearshore zones
Bull Sharks are attracted to areas with reduced salinity (river mouths, harbours) especially post-rainfall
Summer-autumn period (Nov-Apr) shows peak activity, but incidents occur year-round in SE Australia
Turbid/murky water conditions from runoff may actually attract Bull Sharks as they hunt effectively using electroreception

researchPapers.title: Environmental determinants of shark attacks: a review of published data
keyFindings: Water temperature is a significant predictor of shark presence in temperate coastal zones
Seasonal patterns show increased activity during warmer months (Nov-Feb in Southern Hemisphere)
Turbidity from runoff reduces visibility and may increase encounter risk

researchPapers.title: Shark behaviour and ecology in response to environmental variation
keyFindings: Temperature drives seasonal migration patterns for multiple shark species
Nearshore movements increase with water temperatures above 20°C
Environmental fluctuations correlate with changes in habitat use

researchPapers.title: Global patterns and predictions of seafloor biomass using random forests
keyFindings: Swell and wave action influence nearshore prey availability
Moderate swell conditions (1.5-3m) associated with increased predator activity in surf zones

researchPapers.title: Coastal urbanization and marine predator-prey dynamics
keyFindings: Rainfall events increase nutrient runoff, affecting coastal prey distribution
Turbidity from storm water discharge may mask visual predator cues
Urban coastal zones show distinct environmental risk patterns

researchPapers.title: Shark movement patterns and environmental drivers in temperate coastal waters
keyFindings: Sharks exhibit predictable responses to temperature gradients
Summer months correlate with increased nearshore presence
Water quality and visibility impact predator foraging efficiency

researchPapers.title: Environmental factors influencing shark bite incidents
keyFindings: Combination of environmental factors better predicts risk than single variables
Rainfall preceding beach activity increases turbidity and reduces water clarity
Seasonal water temperature is the strongest single predictor

dataProvenance.description: Daily rainfall totals from Sydney Observatory Hill (Station 066062) and regional observation stations
Sea surface temperature from Sydney offshore buoys and coastal stations (Fort Denison and Sydney offshore observations)
Significant wave height from offshore observation buoys in the Sydney region
Water quality is estimated as a proxy based on recent rainfall. Heavy rainfall (>45mm in 48h) is assumed to cause runoff and reduced water clarity/increased turbidity.

disclaimer: This system provides an environmental risk assessment based on known correlations between weather/ocean conditions and shark activity patterns from peer-reviewed research. It is NOT a shark detection or sighting system. The risk levels are heuristic estimates and should be used in conjunction with official beach safety information, lifeguard warnings, and personal judgement. Always swim at patrolled beaches, follow local signage, and never swim alone. The Bureau of Meteorology data used is provided 'as-is' and may be subject to delays or outages.

methodology.overview: This system implements a multi-species shark risk assessment model based on peer-reviewed research. The model calculates risk for multiple shark species (Bull Sharks, White Sharks, Bronze Whalers, and Tiger Sharks), each with unique behavioral patterns and environmental triggers. Species are weighted by their likelihood and incident history at each location to provide accurate, location-specific risk assessment.

conditions.name: Water Temperature
conditions.rationale: Different shark species have different temperature preferences. Bull Sharks favor 18-28°C, White Sharks prefer cooler 12-22°C, Tiger Sharks need warmer 20-30°C+ water. Temperature is a key driver of species presence.

conditions.name: Rainfall (48h)
conditions.rationale: Rainfall has species-specific effects. Bull Sharks are strongly attracted to post-rainfall conditions (estuarine species), while White Sharks are largely unaffected by rainfall patterns.

conditions.name: Swell Height
conditions.rationale: Swell conditions favor different species. Bronze Whalers are most active in surf zones (1.2-2.5m), while White Sharks tolerate higher swell. Bull Sharks prefer calmer estuarine waters.

conditions.name: Season
conditions.rationale: Shark activity varies seasonally by species. Bull Sharks peak in summer (Nov-Apr), White Sharks in winter/spring (May-Oct), Tiger Sharks in peak summer (Dec-Feb). Bronze Whalers are most active Nov-Feb.

conditions.name: Turbidity / Water Clarity
conditions.rationale: Species have different responses to water clarity. Bull Sharks hunt effectively in turbid water (electroreception), while White Sharks prefer clear water for visual hunting. Bronze Whalers have moderate tolerance.

methodology.scoring: Risk is calculated independently for each shark species present at a location using species-specific environmental models. Each species score is then weighted by its likelihood (common/occasional/rare) and incident history (high/moderate/low) at that location. The weighted combination determines overall risk. Location type also affects species scores: harbour/estuary locations favor Bull Sharks, open beaches favor White Sharks and Bronze Whalers. Final scores map to five risk levels: Low (0-20), Moderate (21-40), High (41-60), Severe (61-80), Catastrophic (81-100).
